title: Monitoring Database Activity
subtopics: Monitoring connection usage and long-running operations
learning_outcomes: Describe the purpose and main terms of Monitoring Database Activity.
Use or interpret an appropriate PostgreSQL example connected to active sessions pg_stat_activity.
Identify one edge case and select a safe way to verify the expected result.

content.intro: This lesson focuses on Monitoring Database Activity. Its primary job is to help you operate a PostgreSQL instance by reading evidence from settings, logs, statistics, vacuum and storage tools. The listed PDF subtopics define the coverage expected here; work through them in order and connect each one to an example, edge case and checkable result.
content.why_it_matters: This topic matters because PostgreSQL systems must preserve correct results as data grows and more sessions or services interact with it. Practicing monitoring database activity teaches you to make assumptions explicit, apply the right SQL or operational tool, and verify behavior instead of relying on a demonstration that only worked once.

content_blocks.title: Core idea
content_blocks.text: Keep the problem small: operate a PostgreSQL instance by reading evidence from settings, logs, statistics, vacuum and storage tools. A PostgreSQL feature should be chosen for the semantics it provides, not just because it is available. Before executing a change, state the inputs, expected output and boundary conditions. The example below is intentionally small enough to inspect; it illustrates the idea but is not a substitute for a test against your schema and PostgreSQL version.

items.text: Relate this point to monitoring database activity: define the expected behavior, one edge case, and a query or check that would provide evidence.

items.title: Wait events
items.text: Capture the time, database, role and exact diagnostic; separate the original failure from symptoms before changing settings.

items.title: Query statistics
items.text: Read estimated rows and access paths first; when using EXPLAIN ANALYZE remember it executes the statement.

content_blocks.title: Worked example: Monitoring Database Activity
content_blocks.code:
SELECT pid, usename, state, wait_event_type, wait_event
FROM pg_stat_activity
WHERE datname = current_database()
ORDER BY pid;
content_blocks.expected_output: Lists sessions connected to the current database and their state/wait information, subject to permissions.
content_blocks.safety_note: Read-only query; redact usernames and query text before sharing diagnostics.
content_blocks.run_instructions: Run with suitable monitoring privileges. Review production visibility and privacy policies.
content_blocks.reset_steps: For a read-only SELECT or inspection command, no reset is needed. For DDL/DML, use a disposable database; capture the starting state, run the example, inspect the result, and ROLLBACK or drop the lab objects as appropriate. Do not use production data or credentials.

content_blocks.title: Practical checkpoint
content_blocks.text: Version note: PostgreSQL 18.6 is the primary reference. PostgreSQL 19 beta/development features are not assumed to be stable.

task: Create a short practice artifact for “Monitoring Database Activity”: explain its goal, show one example linked to “Active sessions pg_stat_activity”, state the expected result, and include one edge/failure case and verification method. Use a disposable database or static artifact as appropriate.
hints: Start with the listed subtopics, especially “Active sessions pg_stat_activity”, and describe the expected behavior in your own words.
Run or inspect the smallest example that demonstrates the behavior; do not add unrelated features before it is verified.
When the result surprises you, capture the exact SQL/error, check version and permissions, and change one assumption at a time.
expected_output: A reviewable note or query for Monitoring Database Activity, with an explanation of “Active sessions pg_stat_activity”, expected behavior, and a documented edge-case check.

common_mistakes.problem: Copying the example without checking its assumptions.
common_mistakes.why: Object names, data types, privileges, extensions and data distribution affect database behavior.
common_mistakes.fix: List schema/version assumptions and test with a tiny synthetic dataset first.

common_mistakes.problem: Treating a single successful query as proof of production readiness.
common_mistakes.why: A happy-path result does not test invalid input, concurrent sessions, permissions, recovery or query performance.
common_mistakes.fix: Add one negative/edge case and record the evidence that confirms the expected behavior.

common_mistakes.problem: Making a production change directly from a lesson.
common_mistakes.why: DDL, data updates, role changes and operational commands can affect data or availability.
common_mistakes.fix: Use an isolated lab, reviewed migration, least privilege, rollback/recovery plan and a second-person review for production.

summary: Monitoring Database Activity fits into the broader goal to operate a PostgreSQL instance by reading evidence from settings, logs, statistics, vacuum and storage tools.
Use the curriculum subtopics as a completeness checklist: Active sessions pg_stat_activity, Wait events, Query statistics.
State the schema/version assumptions and verify one normal case plus an edge case before trusting the result.
